title: Preprints: Where They Fit in Today’s Public Access Policy Landscape – PsyArXiv Blog
content:
Abstract:  Preprints are widely recognized as an important part of the open access publishing ecosystem, but how do they fit into rapidly evolving public access policies from funders?

Although preprints typically do not satisfy public access requirements from funders, they remain an important and effective way of publishing research openly. In the absence of policies that mandate or incentivize preprint publishing, their adoption is largely shaped by discipline-specific research culture and the practical advantages offered by this form of publishing.

content: Abstract: The Registry of Open Access Repositories has registered 135 Indian repositories. A systematic assessment design was embraced and the repositories were evaluated by F-UJI tool. Some of the key indicators that were evaluated in the assessment include persistent identifiers, metadata quality, access protocols, interoperability standards and licensing information. title: [2608.16322] Estimating global article processing charges paid to 14 publishers for open access between 2019 and 2025
content: This study presents estimates of the global expenditure on article processing charges (APCs) paid to 14 publishers for open access (OA) between 2019 and 2025. APCs are charged for publishing in fully OA journals (gold) and making individual articles OA in subscription journals (hybrid), but how much is paid, and for which articles, is not publicly known. We therefore curated an open dataset of publicly listed APC prices from 14 academic publishers (ACS, CUP, De Gruyter, EDP, Elsevier, Frontiers, IEEE, IOP, MDPI, OUP, PLOS, Sage, Springer Nature, and Wiley) and combined it with counts of OA articles from OpenAlex. We estimate that $15.08 billion (in 2025 USD) was spent globally on APCs between 2019 and 2025. Adjusted for inflation, annual spending quadrupled from $0.9 billion in 2019 to $3.7 billion in 2025, with >85% concentrated among a few large publishers. Hybrid OA fees exceed gold fees, and the median fee paid is higher than the median price listed for both. content: Abstract: The purpose of this study is to examine whether PlumX Altmetric scores can predict the Scopus citation counts for the field of particle physics, and to examine the relationship between the number of citations received by particle physics highly cited documents in Scopus and their Altmetric scores in PlumX. The sample consists of 103 highly cited documents in Particle Physics indexed during 2000-2019 in Scopus. In order to examine the relationship between Scopus citation counts and PlumX Altmetric scores, Spearman’s correlation test and multiple regression analysis were used. The result of the Spearman’s correlation analysis shows a strong relationship between the number of PlumX citations and Scopus citations. Furthermore, PlumX Captures and PlumX Mentions have a significant relationship with Scopus citation counts, but there is no relationship between PlumX Usage and PlumX social media. The results of regression analysis show that PlumX Citations, Captures, Usage, Mentions, and social media, respectively predict 85, 62, 60, 55, and 47 percent of Scopus citation counts. title: A dataset of article processing charges from 14 scholarly publishers, 2019-2025
content: Abstract:  This paper introduces a dataset of APCs produced from the price lists of 14 large scholarly publishers between 2019 and 2025. APC price lists were downloaded from publisher websites each year as well as via Wayback Machine snapshots to retrieve fees per journal per year. The dataset includes journal metadata, APC collection method, and annual APC price list information in several currencies (USD, EUR, GBP, CHF, JPY, CAD, AUD) for 12,540 unique journals and 69,856 journal-year combinations. The dataset was generated to allow for more precise analysis of APCs and can support library collection development and scientometric analysis estimating APCs paid in gold and hybrid OA journals.

title: Can This Massive, Free Aggregator Platform Compete with Commercial Giants? | Katina Magazine
content: "Scilit stands out for its scope, speed, and openness. But it lacks analytical capabilities and is undermined by the reputation of its parent company.... In the rapidly evolving landscape of modern scientific publishing, tools that index and democratize access to research have become crucial for global academic advancement. Scilit, a free-access content aggregator platform developed and maintained by Multidisciplinary Digital Publishing Institute (MDPI), stands out as an ambitious entry in this arena. In this review, I’ll explore Scilit’s core features, search capabilities, user interface, and integration of automated data extraction tools. By aggregating metadata from open repositories and official registration bodies, Scilit has carved out a distinct niche alongside traditional indexing giants like Web of Science and Scopus. But while Scilit offers impressive scope, rapid ingestion times, and unmatched pricing (entirely free), it faces limitations in advanced filtering, heavy reliance on Crossref’s digital object identifier (DOI) metadata service, metadata standardization, and structural clarity. content: Abstract: Background: Peer-reviewed medical literature consistently violates established health literacy readability targets, creating a gap that effectively excludes patients and caregivers from accessing evidence-based information. Methods:This cross-sectional study analyzed 85 open access, peer-reviewed pediatric strabismus articles published between 2022 and 2025, stratified by strabismus subtype, surgical relevance, and publication type. title: Which Data Repository Should You Use?
content:
"The Center for Open Science has announced that from November 16, 2026, no new projects can be created on the Open Science Framework. After February 19 all projects will become read-only, and eventually, they anticipate that all private projects will be deleted. The OSF has raised a generation of scientists that is able to practice open science. These scientists will need to take these skills to a new data repository in the future....

There are many data repositories, each with their own strengths and weaknesses. Before I compare them, I want to make it clear that the fact that organizations are willing to store your data for free for a very long time is an amazing service. You should be incredibly grateful that any and all of these services exist. As someone who had a free Hotmail email account in 1997 with 2 mb of free storage, the fact that we can now store up to 50GB for every project we create in a data repository blows my mind.

Some common data repositories used in psychology are Zenodo, GitHub, ResearchBox, Dataverse, and PsyArchives. I will compare these services on properties that I think are important."

title: A Graph Approach to the Academic Publishing Network: A Heterogeneous Model and Structural Screening over OpenAlex Open Data
content: Abstract: The academic publishing ecosystem is a vast, heterogeneous network of works, authors, institutions, journals, and topics. Traditional scientometrics reduces it to isolated tabular indicators (h-index, Impact Factor) that ignore topological context and are not designed to capture coordinated illegitimate practices. Building on our companion review, which proposed graph analysis of publishing integrity, this paper implements that approach. We define a heterogeneous multivariate graph model over OpenAlex open data (seven node types, seven edge types) and a methodology based on projections (citation and co-authorship networks), interpretable structural metrics, community detection, and three screening detectors of anomalous publishing patterns. We deliberately avoid binary classification: detectors return ranked candidates with explicit structural evidence for human assessment. On the institutional corpus of VSB - Technical University of Ostrava (2020-2025) with its one-hop citation neighbourhood, community detection recovers real research groups, centralities identify cross-disciplinary bridges, and the screenings flag dense co-authorship cliques, locally closed citation

title: Keldysh Institute of Applied Mathematics’ Preprints: Conversion from MS Word to HTML | Automatic Documentation and Mathematical Linguistics | Springer Nature Link
content: Abstract:  In recent years, the presentation of full-text scientific articles in HTML has become widespread. This format offers several advantages for online publication compared to the traditional PDF format, owing to its more advanced tools for structuring material, embedding multimedia content, and implementing various interactive and dynamic features. Therefore, the task of converting manuscripts from the traditionally used MS Word and LaTeX formats into a high-quality HTML version that is capable of realizing the advantages of this format has become relevant. This paper presents the results of applying the approach for converting scientific articles from MS Word to HTML, proposed in previous studies, to Keldysh Institute of Applied Mathematics’ preprints. The interactive capabilities of the resulting HTML versions are described.

title: Can low-cost, open-access journals from the Global South have a high impact? Can low-cost, open-access journals from the Global South have a high impact?
content: Abstract: This study examines whether Brazilian journals indexed in SciELO can achieve significant academic and policy impact. The 20,000 most-cited documents, out of 368,000 papers found in Scopus, were evaluated. These articles, especially in health and agricultural sciences, had citation impacts more than twice the global average. The impact was strongly influenced by the journal’s quartile ranking and publisher type, with Q1 journals and those managed by associations or commercial publishers outperforming those in other quartiles. Impactful papers also frequently came from institutional and university publishers. SciELO publications have relevance beyond academia, as evidenced by their citations in major policy documents issued by the WHO, UNESCO, FAO, and Brazilian government agencies. These were associated with significantly higher academic impact. Leading pharmaceutical and technology firms referenced these papers in patent filings. International collaboration was limited and did not significantly influence citation rates. content:
"Introduction to the Nepali Language is the first free open-access textbook of its kind designed for learners, educators, community groups, and heritage speakers of Nepali.  The book was launched in celebration of BC’s first-ever Nepali Heritage Day on 30 May, 2026, marking an important milestone in expanding opportunities for Nepali language learning and engagement.

Developed within the Faculty of Arts, the textbook was created through a collaboration between faculty, students, and staff. The team included principal investigator Dr. Mark Turin, an Associate Professor in the Department of Anthropology and the Institute for Critical Indigenous Studies; Binod Shrestha, an instructor with the Himalaya Program; and Salina Dolmo Lama, a Nepali graduate student at the School of Public Policy and Global Affairs.

title: Investing $4.9 million of our surplus in rebuilding the Crossref system - Crossref
content:
"The infrastructure that registers and distributes Crossref metadata has been running and growing for more than two decades. It now does considerably more than it was built to do, and it shows: two large, tightly coupled monoliths (Content System and REST API), where a change in one place risks breaking something in another.

In its July meeting, the Crossref board approved the use of Crossref surplus funds for a three-year project to accelerate the redesign of the Crossref system. Our plan is to use $1.6 million a year for three years (~USD $4.9M in total) from our surplus funds, which will help us set up a modern infrastructure consisting of separate services for the different functionalities that the Crossref system offers."

title: Not All Research Environments are Created Equal: Structural Injustice in Low-Resourced Scientific Settings and Its Epistemic Implications
content: Abstract: This paper discusses three forms of structural injustice associated with disparities in the resources available to researchers, and the opportunity researchers have to pursue their scientific goals. These are: (1) resource injustice; (2) focus injustice; and (3) labour injustice. I argue that such structural injustice has significant epistemic implications, resulting in: shifts in research content; the exclusion of substantive portions of scientific community from contributing to knowledge production to the best of their abilities; the exclusion of specific methods and data sources from global scientific discourse, on grounds other than scientific quality and relevance; a loss of quality and reliability in processes and outcomes of inquiry; and the inability to implement openness and related forms of constructive scrutiny. To exemplify these forms of injustice and their epistemic implications, I discuss everyday challenges within life science sites in Italy, Ghana and Greece, as documented through ethnographic research. title: Knowledge Engineering for Open Science: Building and Deploying Knowledge Bases for Metadata Standards - Musen - 2026 - AI Magazine - Wiley Online Library
content: Abstract: For more than a decade, scientists have been striving to make their datasets available in open repositories, with the goal that they be findable, accessible, interoperable, and reusable (FAIR). Although it is hard for most investigators to remember all the “guiding principles” associated with FAIR data, there is one overarching requirement: The data need to be annotated with “rich,” discipline-specific, standardized metadata that can enable third parties to understand who performed the experiment, who or what the subjects were, what the experimental conditions were, and what the results appear to show. Most areas of science lack standards for such metadata and, when such standards exist, it can be difficult for investigators or data curators to apply them. content: "But given the many different ways to connect in the Fediverse—why do almost all academic associations or institutions choose a Mastodon server, of all things, for their communities? Bonfire isn’t a platform or an “app,” but rather a modular framework for building digital community spaces. Possible features include feeds (that interact with or federate with Mastodon, etc.), groups, user circles, and moderation tools… and if something is missing, you can develop it (or have it developed). title: Open practices across science, software, education and other domains | Nature Human Behaviour
content: Abstract:  Open practices are actions people perform to influence transparency (who can see information), inclusion (who can voice perspectives) and decision rights (who can make decisions). Open practices have grown popular across domains, including open science, open-source software and open education, in hopes of spurring innovation and broadening participation. But which open practices best enable groups and organizations to achieve these ambitious goals, and why? This Perspective distils seven successful practices from across these domains that can help groups to define goals, allocate power, share information and set norms. These practices, such as documenting power structures and adopting a code of conduct, hold potential to support groups and organizations seeking to address great challenges through openness. However, delivering on that potential will depend on how well groups share lessons across domains, tailor these practices and sustain the people and platforms that carry them.

title: On the Open Science Framework's changes - Chris Hartgerink, PhD
content:
"The OSF was pivotal to the early days of reforming research around 2012-2017. I used it a lot for a while, and ultimately used it through its integrations only. It added some great services and some not so great ones. I did not always agree with their approach, but I was often glad they existed.

The OSF has had many failings over the years and I think it is great they're making a decision on the role it has in 2026 and beyond. To me, the decision to unwind projects is a reflection of the fact that they did not really connect with the userbase to understand the needs of researchers, while riding on the tide that they served the researcher's needs. They gobbled up tens of millions of dollars for their operations. The fact that this announcement came as a surprise, is a highlight of how disconnected the development was from the people they claim to serve."

title: OSF is Changing: What's changing, what's continuing, and where to find guidance
content: "We are preparing substantial changes to OSF that will reduce its functionality, focus OSF on its unique strengths, and move toward an integrated model with complementary services like Zenodo, a repository for researchers to share data, materials, and code hosted by CERN, for researchers to do open science. As part of that shift, the OSF Projects workflow – the part of the OSF used for project collaboration, file management, and storage – is being phased out as an active workspace. This change does not affect persistence and accessibility of existing public projects. We are very sorry for the disruption that this will cause for OSF users. These changes are necessary because of a challenging funding environment for open research infrastructure. Important background about why we are making this change is available in a separate post. Our priorities are to support the long-term discovery and access of content publicly shared on OSF so it remains persistent, discoverable, and accessible, and to ease the transition for users to continue doing open science. title: Librarians as Creators of Open Educational Resources for Advanced Searching
content: Abstract:  Health librarians are increasingly authoring their own open educational resources (OERs) to teach advanced literature searching—an essential skill for evidence synthesis. These instructional materials, often created in response to gaps in existing resources, go beyond simple guides incorporating bilingual content, scaffolded exercises, knowledge checks, and video tutorials. They reflect librarians’ deep expertise and commitment to affordable, open, and high-quality learning materials. This panel will explore three librarian-led OER projects that exemplify this growing trend. Through brief presentations and a moderated discussion, panelists will share insights into the design, implementation, and impact of their work, and reflect on the broader implications of OER creation as a scholarly and pedagogical practice.

title: University libraries between cost-cutting measures and open access transformation
content: From Google's English:  “When considering the financial resources of university libraries, two fundamental developments must be distinguished, both of which impact their budgets,” explains André Karliczek, Deputy Director of the Thuringian University and State Library Jena (ThULB). “Firstly, these libraries, whose core mission is providing information for study, research, and teaching, are increasingly becoming the primary bearers of publication costs in the course of the open access transformation – particularly within the framework of the DEAL agreements – because publishers have shifted their business model from subscription to open access publication. Acquisition budgets are therefore no longer solely used to purchase and license literature, but increasingly also to finance publication fees. title: Beyond metric reductionism: assessment creep as an emerging risk of research evaluation reform | Research Evaluation | Oxford Academic
content: Abstract:  Recent research assessment reforms have successfully challenged the overreliance on simplistic quantitative indicators and promoted broader approaches to evaluation. This paper argues that these reforms may also generate a new risk: assessment creep, understood as the gradual accumulation of evaluation criteria without sufficient attention to how they are prioritised and combined. While criteria such as open science, societal impact, international collaboration, leadership, and mentoring may each be valuable, their proliferation can reduce transparency and make evaluation systems more difficult to understand and scrutinise. Less transparent systems may also make it harder to distinguish legitimate expert judgement from arbitrary decision-making and to detect favouritism or other forms of unwarranted advantage. Drawing on recent debates surrounding responsible research assessment, the paper suggests that the next challenge is not choosing between metrics and expert judgement, but designing evaluation systems that remain coherent, transparent, and accountable as they become increasingly complex.

Over the past decade, widespread use of TOP 2015 contributed to valuable evidence and feedback for refinement.Main TextThe TOP Advisory Board undertook a comprehensive update of TOP 2015 that went into effect in 2025 (TOP 2025). title: How a Diamond Open Access Publisher Expanded into Open Textbooks - Pressbooks
content:
The University of Groningen Press (UGP) is a Diamond Open Access university press based in the Netherlands and a member of the Netherlands University Presses (NUPs) network. Since its founding in 2017, the press has supported the publication of Diamond Open Access scholarly journals and books.

In 2021, UGP expanded into a closely related—but distinct—area of open publishing by launching an open textbook pilot. As part of the University’s broader commitment to open education and open science, the initiative explored how UGP could apply its scholarly publishing expertise and open infrastructure to help faculty create high-quality open textbooks and other open educational resources.

What began as a pilot has since developed into an institutional service supporting multiple models of textbook production, enabling collaboration across institutions, and supporting the creation of interactive learning materials designed for teaching and learning contexts.

title: Panel: Hoe maken we Open Science echt gelijkwaardig?
content: How can science and knowledge production become more open, inclusive and equitable? This is not only a question of access to existing knowledge, but also of agency: who formulates research questions, who is recognised as a knowledge producer, and which forms of knowledge are considered legitimate? During the Netherlands National Open Science Week, Leiden University’s three UNESCO Chairs will come together to discuss these questions. The Chairs maintain broad international networks and collaborate with researchers and knowledge communities in Africa, Asia and Latin America. Their work covers diversity in science, digital diversity, colonial history, and collaboration with societal and international knowledge communities. The central question of the panel is how researchers, universities and research funders can contribute to more equitable international collaboration. The panellists will also critically examine the distribution of resources, authorship, theoretical authority and institutional recognition. title: Risks and possibilities in sharing preprints during the doctorate - University of Southern Denmark
content: Abstract:  During doctoral candidature, students may seek to publish journal articles, which they may incorporate in their thesis if their institutional policy permits. They may consider sharing pre-prints of these texts either pre- or post-publication to promote open access and knowledge mobilisation. There is very little extant research that explores doctoral students’ knowledge of the risks and possibilities involved in sharing their work in this form, and this chapter seeks to identify those that they could encounter. It offers immediate value for informing doctoral education and a useful foundation for future research that is specific to the doctoral student experience.
